title: Diaspora and Soft Power

cards.h: People and culture as foreign policy
cards.b:
India has the world's largest diaspora, over 30 million people, and a rich cultural brand. Both feed foreign policy: remittances, political influence, goodwill and knowledge. UPSC asks about diaspora policy and about soft power, often with examples.

Expect this as a 10 or 15 mark question, or as a supporting example inside a longer answer. Read the cards in order, then test yourself with the quiz.
Categories: NRI (Indian citizen abroad), PIO (person of Indian origin), OCI (overseas citizen of India; PIO merged into OCI in 2015).

• 1983: Emigration Act (protection of workers).
  • 2000-01: L.M. Singhvi High Level Committee.
  • 2003: Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (9 January, in memory of Gandhi's return in 1915).
  • 2004: Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs, merged into the MEA in 2016.
  • 2005: OCI card. 2014+: Madad, e-Migrate, MADAD portal, PBD held every two years from 2015.

India is the top recipient of remittances: about 125 billion US dollars in 2023 (World Bank), over a tenth of global flows, largely from the US, UAE, UK, Saudi Arabia and Singapore. The diaspora drives investment and technology links. The Indian-American community helped win support for the India-US nuclear deal (2008) and holds high office (such as the vice-presidents in some states). In the UK, Singapore and Mauritius, Indian-origin leaders have headed governments.

India's evacuations: Operation Raahat (Yemen, 2015), Vande Bharat Mission (2020, Covid), Operation Ganga (Ukraine, 2022), Operation Kaveri (Sudan, 2023), Operation Ajay (Israel, 2023). Issues: Gulf kafala labour system, wage theft, deaths, and trafficking. Remittance dependence makes Kerala, Punjab and Gulf links politically sensitive.

Keep the name, the year and the one-line claim ready. These three details are what examiners look for when they check a concept.

Joseph Nye (1990) defined soft power as getting what you want by attraction, not coercion, through culture, values and policies. India's assets: yoga (International Day of Yoga on 21 June, UNGA 2014, first marked 2015), Buddhism and Buddhist circuits, Ayurveda, Bollywood and cuisine, democracy and diversity, ICCR (1950), ITEC and development aid, millets (UN International Year of Millets, 2023), and the Gandhian brand.

• Soft power must be matched by policy credibility and human rights records.
  • Diaspora activism can strain ties: Khalistan-linked groups, the 2023 Canada row after the Nijjar killing.
  • Domestic social tensions and press freedom concerns affect India's image.
  • Gulf workers are vulnerable; skilled migration causes 'brain drain' (or 'brain gain' by remittances and returns).
  • Some diaspora groups carry domestic politics abroad.

China uses Confucius Institutes and the Belt and Road; the US uses universities, Hollywood and the dollar; Japan its 'Cool Japan'; Israel and Ireland engage diasporas intensively. India's special advantage: a large, educated, English-speaking diaspora and a plural cultural heritage. 'Diaspora diplomacy' is a Modi-era phrase.

Priorities: safer migration and labour agreements, skill and language training, student protection, link the diaspora with investment (Start-up India), preserve culture in new generations, and promote culture through the Indian Council for Cultural Relations and 'Study in India'. For essays, argue that soft and hard power reinforce each other.

"Examine the role of the Indian diaspora in India's foreign policy."
"What is soft power? Assess the soft-power assets of India."
"What challenges do Indian workers in the Gulf face and how has India responded?"

Structure: definition, categories, policy, economic weight, protection, soft power, limits, way forward.
